Mind controlled robotic arm

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Scientists design a prosthetic arm that can be controlled by thinking

Unique Selling Point:
Amazing breakthrough technology

Summary:
Physicians and biomedical engineers from Johns Hopkins report what they believe is the first successful effort to wiggle fingers individually and independently of each other using a mind-controlled artificial “arm” to control the movement.

Further information:
Mind-Controlled Prosthetic Arm Moves Individual ‘Fingers’
Physicians and biomedical engineers from Johns Hopkins report what they believe is the first successful effort to wiggle fingers individually and independently of each other using a mind-controlled artificial “arm” to control the movement.
The proof-of-concept feat, described online this week in the Journal of Neural Engineering, represents a potential advance in technologies to restore refined hand function to those who have lost arms to injury or disease, the researchers say. The young man on whom the experiment was performed was not missing an arm or hand, but he was outfitted with a device that essentially took advantage of a brain-mapping procedure to bypass control of his own arm and hand.
“We believe this is the first time a person using a mind-controlled prosthesis has immediately performed individual digit movements without extensive training,” says senior author Nathan Crone, M.D., professor of neurology at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine. “This technology goes beyond available prostheses, in which the artificial digits, or fingers, moved as a single unit to make a grabbing motion, like one used to grip a tennis ball.
For the experiment, the research team recruited a young man with epilepsy already scheduled to undergo brain mapping at The Johns Hopkins Hospital’s Epilepsy Monitoring Unit to pinpoint the origin of his seizures.
While brain recordings were made using electrodes surgically implanted for clinical reasons, the signals also control a modular prosthetic limb developed by the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory.
Prior to connecting the prosthesis, the researchers mapped and tracked the specific parts of the subject’s brain responsible for moving each finger, then programmed the prosthesis to move the corresponding finger.
First, the patient’s neurosurgeon placed an array of 128 electrode sensors — all on a single rectangular sheet of film the size of a credit card — on the part of the man’s brain that normally controls hand and arm movements. Each sensor measured a circle of brain tissue 1 millimeter in diameter.
The computer program the Johns Hopkins team developed had the man move individual fingers on command and recorded which parts of the brain the “lit up” when each sensor detected an electric signal.
In addition to collecting data on the parts of brain involved in motor movement, the researchers measured electrical brain activity involved in tactile sensation. To do this, the subject was outfitted with a glove with small, vibrating buzzers in the fingertips, which went off individually in each finger. The researchers measured the resulting electrical activity in the brain for each finger connection.
After the motor and sensory data were collected, the researchers programmed the prosthetic arm to move corresponding fingers based on which part of the brain was active. The researchers turned on the prosthetic arm, which was wired to the patient through the brain electrodes, and asked the subject to “think” about individually moving thumb, index, middle, ring and pinkie fingers. The electrical activity generated in the brain moved the fingers.
“The electrodes used to measure brain activity in this study gave us better resolution of a large region of cortex than anything we’ve used before and allowed for more precise spatial mapping in the brain,” says Guy Hotson, graduate student and lead author of the study. “This precision is what allowed us to separate the control of individual fingers.”
Initially, the mind-controlled limb had an accuracy of 76 percent. Once the researchers coupled the ring and pinkie fingers together, the accuracy increased to 88 percent.
“The part of the brain that controls the pinkie and ring fingers overlaps, and most people move the two fingers together,” says Crone. “It makes sense that coupling these two fingers improved the accuracy.”
The researchers note there was no pre-training required for the subject to gain this level of control, and the entire experiment took less than two hours.
Crone cautions that application of this technology to those actually missing limbs is still some years off and will be costly, requiring extensive mapping and computer programming. According to the Amputee Coalition, over 100,000 people living in the U.S. have amputated hands or arms, and most could potentially benefit from such technology.
Additional authors on the study include David McMullen, Matthew Fifer, William Anderson and Nitish Thakor of Johns Hopkins Medicine and Matthew Johannes, Kapil Katyal, Matthew Para, Robert Armiger and Brock Wester of the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory.
This study was funded by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (grant number 1R01NS088606-01).

Press Release:


Mind-controlled Prosthetic Arm
Just by thinking about moving his non-existent limb, a double amputee controls a cutting-edge robotic arm. Carte Blanche meets the Johns Hopkins University scientists who have turned neural signals from an amputee’s brain into commands that move the prosthetic limb. Set to fundamentally change the lives of amputees and paralysed people, this is the most sophisticated prosthetic arm in the world.


Script:


V/O:
This is the most sophisticated prosthetic arm in the world. It moves just like the real thing…… It is a marvel of modern biomedical engineering... And unlike any other prosthetic arm its fingers can move individually…... Sadly, it has its origins in events such as these……..
Link:
During the Iraq and Afghanistan conflicts improvised explosive devices killed and maimed tens of thousands of US soldiers and many of them lost an arm or leg.
V/O:
In 2006 the US Department of Defence requested Johns Hopkins University to design a revolutionary prosthetic arm for military amputees.
Brock:
DARPA, the Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency was the sponsor on the effort and they had a very specific set of capabilities in mind when they created the programme
V/O:
Brock Wester is a biomedical engineer at the Applied Physics Lab or APL at Johns Hopkins University. In two thousand and six they started to develop something completely unprecedented.
Brock:
It had to have the same form factor as a human hand, it had to weigh the same, and it had to have the same speed, the same range of motion. And so, to engineer something that can move like the human arm, it is very complicated. The motors didn’t exist at the time for the fingers. They were too big so we had to make custom motors. We had to define new ways to programme movement so that it was fluid, humanlike. The sensors in the hand that help the control system move the limb; all custom.
V/O:
The arm was also to be modular and could include either a hand or a hand and forearm or even a whole arm.
LINK:
The arm is controlled by electrical impulses that are sent to it. Certain combinations of impulses result in certain movements.
V/O:
When we visited Johns Hopkins, biomedical engineer Guy Hotson demonstrated the arm. Impulses in finger nerves are picked up by the glove and sent to a computer that translates them into movements of a physical or virtual arm on screen.

The sensors on his arm pick up electric impulses in the nerves of the arm and send them to the computer.
UPSOUND: GUY
There is a classifier, an algorithm that is looking at the signals while performing those movements and then it is able to kind of learn “Hey, this is what the signals kind of look like when I was doing this movement and this is what they look like when they’re just resting.
V/O:
The signals originate in the brain. When we think about moving an arm or leg, neurons fire in our brain’s motor cortex and send an array of signals, via the nerves, to the muscles in a limb to make it move.
LINK:
And even if a person has had an amputation and thinks about moving a missing arm, the same array of neurons fires and sends impulses through the nerves right up to where the amputation happened.
V/O:
The team at Johns Hopkins have designed sensors that can detect these electrical impulses and also created software that can use the impulses to control the prosthetic arm. Johnny Matheny, who lost his arm, has an implant on the bone in his stump to enable the attachment of a prosthetic limb. When he thinks about moving his missing arm, neurons fire in his brain and send impulses down the nerves. Sensors on his stump pick up these signals and a computer translates them into commands to the prosthetic limb. So, simply by thinking Johnny is controlling the arm.
Johnny Matheny
The APL arm is the most unique arm. It has the ability to do anything that your natural hand, wrist, elbow, shoulder can do.
V/O:
Leslie Baugh is a double shoulder amputee. Here, sensors are placed over areas where they will be able to pick up his brain signals when he thinks about moving his non-existent arms or fingers.

Simply thinking about moving an arm causes his brain to send signals that activate the prosthetic arm.

Fitted with a special brace, he is able to work with two functioning limbs. With some practice he is even able to control the fingers through thought.
Leslie Baugh:
Once the training sessions were complete and they released me and let me be the computer to control that arm, I just go into a whole different world
LINK
So, the technology they had developed could tap into the signals from the brain via nerves that remained after the amputation. It worked well, but they wanted to take it even further.
Brock:
So at that point the focus of the programme, which originally was working with amputee subjects had shifted to focus on neural control or brain computer-interface control. So most of the subjects at that point, individuals were quadriplegia and other neuro muscular and neuro-degenerative disorders. So they couldn’t move their limbs.
V/O:
But even completely paralysed people’s neurons fire in the same way as able-bodied people’s neurons when they think about moving say, an arm. It is just that the signals remain contained in the brain.
LINK:
The scientists knew that if they could find a way to access the signals directly in the brain instead at nerves where there were amputations, they would have a shot at controlling the prosthetic arm with these impulses alone.
V/O:
And at Johns Hopkins there was somebody who could make this possible. Prof Nathan Crone is a neurologist specializing in epilepsy and mapping of brain activity in epileptics.
Prof Nathan Crone:
What we have been doing here at Hopkins for a number of years now is to use just passive recordings of the normal activity of the brain while patients are performing tasks such as speaking. So we’ve been mapping language cortex in this way for a number of years and also mapping motor-cortex.
LINK:
And having access to the brain impulses in the motor cortex was what the prosthetic arm team needed.
V/O:
Nathan records brain signals by placing sensors directly onto the surface of an epileptic patient’s brain during a surgical procedure. The sensors remain on the brain for a week or two while the patient is monitored.
Crone:
We are trying to record their seizures to pinpoint exactly where the seizures are coming from but also it is just as important that we are mapping the function of their brains.
V/O:
An additional credit card-sized array of sensors was placed onto the motor cortex of volunteers among Nathan’s patients. This enabled his team to make additional recordings of neural signals linked to arm and hand movement.
Guy:
We looked at the movement that the patient was making with their fingers and then we looked at the changes in their neural signals and how those relate. After teaching the computer how these two things relate we can actually stream the signals to the computer.
LINK:
The computer can then command the prosthetic arm to make certain movements. This allows the patients to take control of the arm using just their thoughts. Completely paralysed people will also be able to control the arm through an implant on the brain.
V/O:
A recent innovation is the addition of sensors to the hand and fingers that can send signals back to the brain.
Brock:
A big part of moving our limbs and interacting with objects in real world settings is the ability to sense and touch things and feel that tactile contact as we work with objects. Without that sensory feedback during movement individuals really lose a lot of dexterity and capability.
V/O:
For now the APL arm is a prototype and not commercially available, but the team we met is confident that what they are doing will change the lives of amputees and paralysed people fundamentally in future.
Johnny Matheny:
Now Johnny is in his environment. Get out of my kitchen. I’m going to town.

For the experiment, the research team recruited a young man with epilepsy already scheduled to undergo brain mapping at The Johns Hopkins Hospital’s Epilepsy Monitoring Unit to pinpoint the origin of his seizures. While brain recordings were made using electrodes surgically implanted for clinical reasons, the signals also control a modular prosthetic limb developed by the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory. Prior to connecting the prosthesis, the researchers mapped and tracked the specific parts of the subject’s brain responsible for moving each finger, then programmed the prosthesis to move the corresponding finger. First, the patient’s neurosurgeon placed an array of 128 electrode sensors — all on a single rectangular sheet of film the size of a credit card — on the part of the man’s brain that normally controls hand and arm movements. Each sensor measured a circle of brain tissue 1 millimeter in diameter. The computer program the Johns Hopkins team developed had the man move individual fingers on command and recorded which parts of the brain the “lit up” when each sensor detected an electric signal. In addition to collecting data on the parts of brain involved in motor movement, the researchers measured electrical brain activity involved in tactile sensation. To do this, the subject was outfitted with a glove with small, vibrating buzzers in the fingertips, which went off individually in each finger. The researchers measured the resulting electrical activity in the brain for each finger connection. After the motor and sensory data were collected, the researchers programmed the prosthetic arm to move corresponding fingers based on which part of the brain was active. The researchers turned on the prosthetic arm, which was wired to the patient through the brain electrodes, and asked the subject to “think” about individually moving thumb, index, middle, ring and pinkie fingers. The electrical activity generated in the brain moved the fingers. “The electrodes used to measure brain activity in this study gave us better resolution of a large region of cortex than anything we’ve used before and allowed for more precise spatial mapping in the brain,” says Guy Hotson, graduate student and lead author of the study. “This precision is what allowed us to separate the control of individual fingers.” Initially, the mind-controlled limb had an accuracy of 76 percent. Once the researchers coupled the ring and pinkie fingers together, the accuracy increased to 88 percent. “The part of the brain that controls the pinkie and ring fingers overlaps, and most people move the two fingers together,” says Crone. “It makes sense that coupling these two fingers improved the accuracy.” The researchers note there was no pre-training required for the subject to gain this level of control, and the entire experiment took less than two hours. Crone cautions that application of this technology to those actually missing limbs is still some years off and will be costly, requiring extensive mapping and computer programming. According to the Amputee Coalition, over 100,000 people living in the U.S. have amputated hands or arms, and most could potentially benefit from such technology. Additional authors on the study include David McMullen, Matthew Fifer, William Anderson and Nitish Thakor of Johns Hopkins Medicine and Matthew Johannes, Kapil Katyal, Matthew Para, Robert Armiger and Brock Wester of the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory. This study was funded by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (grant number 1R01NS088606-01).
